title: Count Safe Queen Layouts
statement:
Place n chess queens on an n × n board so that no two of them attack each other: no two share a row, a column, or a diagonal (in either direction).

Return how many different layouts exist. Two layouts are different if some square holds a queen in one and not in the other; mirrored or rotated copies count separately.

examples.why: Queens in columns 1, 3, 0, 2 (one per row, top to bottom), and its mirror image 2, 0, 3, 1.
In the centre, the middle-row queen attacks every square above and below it. On an edge, it leaves one safe square in the top row and one in the bottom row, and those two share a column.
A single queen on a single square attacks nothing.

hints: Every row holds exactly one queen. So decide row by row which column gets the queen.
When placing a queen in row r, column c, you only need to know which columns and which diagonals are already taken. Squares on one diagonal share r − c; on the other, r + c.
Backtrack: keep three sets (columns, r − c, r + c), try each free column, recurse to the next row, and undo. Count the times you reach row n.

explain.intuition:
Since queens attack along rows, each row has exactly one queen, which turns the search into choosing a column per row. Fill rows top to bottom and stop a branch as soon as the new queen is attacked. Most branches die within a few rows, which is why the search is fast even though there are nn raw column choices.

The check itself can be O(1). All squares on a "\" diagonal share the value row − col, and all squares on a "/" diagonal share row + col. Keep the used columns and both kinds of diagonal in sets (or bitmasks), and a square is safe exactly when none of its three keys are taken. You only count, so there is no board to copy or print.
steps: Recurse on row, starting at 0, with three empty sets: cols, diag (row − col) and anti (row + col).
If row === n, one full layout is found: return 1.
Otherwise, for each column c not blocked in any set, add its three keys, add the result of recursing on row + 1 to a total, and remove the keys.
Return the total. With bitmasks, the free columns for the next row are ~(cols | diag | anti) after shifting the diagonal masks by one.
pitfalls: Checking only one diagonal direction. Both "\" and "/" diagonals are attack lines.
Forgetting to remove the keys after the recursive call, so later branches see queens that are no longer there.
Dividing by symmetry (e.g. counting half and doubling). It breaks for odd n, where the middle column has no mirror partner.

complexity.time: O(n!) in the worst case, far less in practice

solutions.title: Backtracking with a scan of earlier rows
solutions.idea: Place one queen per row and check the new queen against every queen above it.

solutions.title: Backtracking with column and diagonal sets
solutions.idea: A square is free when its column, its row − col and its row + col are all unused. Three sets make the check O(1).

solutions.title: Bitmask backtracking
solutions.idea: Hold the blocked columns of the current row in three bitmasks. Shifting the diagonal masks by one moves them to the next row.

followups: Return the layouts themselves as boards of '.' and 'Q'.
Use the left-right mirror symmetry to halve the work. How do you handle the middle column when n is odd?
